content: Root canal treatment is performed on teeth where irreversible pulpitis has caused the dental pulp to become necrotic. This procedure serves as an alternative to tooth extraction. The process involves mechanical preparation and irrigation of the root canal using antiseptic or antibacterial solutions to eliminate bacteria and clean the infected area. The ideal irrigant should effectively deactivate bacteria throughout the entire root canal system without inducing adverse tissue reactions. Sodium hypochlorite (NaOCl) and chlorhexidine are commonly used irrigants, but there is ongoing uncertainty regarding which solution, concentration, or combination is most effective. The objective of this review was to evaluate the effects of different irrigants used in non-surgical root canal treatment for mature permanent teeth. To achieve this, a comprehensive search was conducted across multiple databases, including the Cochrane Oral Health Group's Trials Register, CENTRAL, MEDLINE, EMBASE, and LILACS, up to July 5, 2012. No restrictions were placed on language or publication date. The review included randomized controlled trials involving singleor multi-rooted permanent teeth with pulpal or periapical pathology requiring root canal treatment. Comparisons were made between different irrigants, inactive irrigants, or placebos. Combinations of irrigants were also considered, including those used alongside chelating agents like EDTA. Two authors independently assessed the risk of bias in the included trials and extracted relevant data. A total of 11 trials, involving 851 participants and 879 teeth, were included in the review. Of these, two trials were deemed to have a low risk of bias, six had unclear risk, and three had a high risk of bias. Four trials compared sodium hypochlorite with chlorhexidine. However, none of these trials reported primary outcomes, and only two reported a secondary outcome—bacterial growth cultures. In these two trials, 20% and 50% of teeth in the control groups showed positive bacterial cultures. A meta-analysis of these trials found no strong evidence of a difference in bacterial growth between the two interventions (risk ratio 0.73; 95% confidence interval 0.34 to 1.56; P = 0.41). The remaining seven trials each compared different interventions. Only two of these trials provided usable data on primary outcomes, such as swelling and pain. One trial compared sodium hypochlorite 5.25% alone, sodium hypochlorite 5.25% combined with hydrogen peroxide 3%, and normal saline. This trial reported pain levels at 3 to 14 days post-procedure but found no significant difference in pain between the groups. Another trial compared sodium hypochlorite 5% with sodium hypochlorite combined with a proteolytic enzyme and found no significant difference in swelling between the groups. Two additional trials reported bacterial growth outcomes, while three trials did not provide any data that could be used in the review. None of the included trials reported adverse effects or radiological changes in periapical radiolucency. The authors concluded that while irrigants like sodium hypochlorite and chlorhexidine appear to reduce bacterial cultures compared to saline, the majority of studies in this review did not adequately report clinically significant or patient-relevant outcomes. There is insufficient reliable evidence to establish the superiority of any single irrigant. The quality and reliability of the evidence varied, and clinicians should recognize that changes in bacterial counts or early postoperative pain may not accurately predict long-term treatment success. Future research should focus on reporting both clinician-relevant and patient-centered outcomes at well-defined perioperative and long-term time points.
